name: Lenskart
summary: Lenskart sells eyeglasses, sunglasses and contact lenses online and through its own stores, and it runs its own lens and frame manufacturing. Candidates commonly report coding and design rounds for technology roles, and case, analytics or role-play rounds for retail, store and business roles, often about connecting the online and in-store experience.
rounds: Coding or problem-solving round for technology roles
System design or project deep dive for experienced engineers
Case, analytics or role-play round for business, retail and store roles (often)
looks_for: Speed and a willingness to experiment
Learning quickly from experiments that fail
Care for the customer across the app, website and stores
Comfort with retail data: footfall, conversion, returns, repeat purchase

questions.text: Tell me about an experiment you ran that failed. What did you learn, and what did you do next?
covers: What you tested and what you expected
How you knew it failed, and how quickly
What you tried next because of what you learned

questions.text: Describe a time you moved quickly to ship something. How did you keep the quality acceptable?
covers: Why speed mattered
What you checked and what you consciously left for later
The result and the follow-up work

questions.text: Tell me about a time you took ownership of a result that wasn't formally yours.
covers: The result at risk and why you stepped in
What you did and how you worked with the actual owner
The outcome

questions.text: Tell me about a time you handled a difficult customer face to face.
covers: What the customer was upset about
How you listened and what you offered
How it ended, and what you'd do the same next time

questions.text: How would you design a virtual try-on feature that shows frames on a customer's face through the phone camera?
covers: Face tracking to place a 3D frame model correctly as the head moves
Running smoothly on low-cost phones, with a fallback using photos
Privacy: what's processed on the phone and what's stored

questions.text: A customer orders glasses online with a prescription. Walk me through the systems needed to make and deliver them.
covers: Capturing and checking the prescription and lens choices
Routing the order to manufacturing, quality checks and packing
Shipping, tracking and handling a remake if something is wrong

questions.text: Store sales in one city are flat while online sales there keep growing. How would you investigate?
covers: Footfall versus conversion versus order value in stores
Whether online is taking sales from stores or growing the market
Store-level differences: staff, stock, location, local competition

questions.text: How would you decide where to open the next few stores in a city?
covers: Demand signals: online orders by area, footfall, income levels
Rent, visibility and distance from existing stores
Starting with a few, measuring and adjusting the plan

questions.text: How would you reduce returns from customers whose glasses don't fit or don't suit them?
covers: Finding the main return reasons from data and customer comments
Fixes before purchase: try-on, size guidance, better photos
Fixes after: easy adjustments in stores, and tracking the return rate

questions.text: How would you keep inventory accurate across warehouses, stores and the website?
covers: One source of truth updated by every sale, transfer and return
Regular stock counts and reconciling differences
Buffers so the website doesn't sell what a store can't supply

questions.text: A customer in a store is unsure about spending more on lenses. How would you help them choose without pushing?
covers: Asking about their prescription, screen time and lifestyle first
Explaining options and trade-offs in plain words
Respecting their budget and decision

questions.text: Why Lenskart? What do you think it does differently from a traditional optician?
covers: Something specific: the store-plus-online model, technology or own manufacturing
What that changes for customers
What you'd like to contribute

questions.text: Have you used Lenskart's app or visited a store? What would you improve?
covers: A specific moment in the journey
One improvement and who it helps
How you'd test it

questions.text: Some roles involve working in stores, on weekends, or moving to another city. How do you feel about that?
covers: An honest answer about weekends and relocation
Any retail or customer-facing experience
Why the role is worth it to you

tips: Visit a store and browse the app before the interview, and notice how online and offline connect: try-on, eye tests, store pickup.
For business cases, use retail metrics: footfall, conversion, average order value, repeat purchase and returns.
Show speed with judgement: what you'd test small first, and how you'd know to scale it.
For tech roles, think about performance on low-cost phones and patchy networks.
